cues.text: Let us now turn to the third chapter of this study session: cryptography, TLS, IPsec and SSH.
We begin with the building blocks of cryptography.
First, symmetric encryption.
In symmetric encryption, both parties use a shared secret, the same key, to protect and to recover the data.
The standard example is AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard.
The practical challenge is that both sides must already hold that shared secret.
Asymmetric cryptography works differently.
Instead of one shared secret, each party has a pair of keys: a public key and a private key.
The public key can be shared openly; the private key is kept secret.
The source gives two example uses: signatures, and key agreement, which is a way for two parties to arrive at shared keys.
Next, the cryptographic hash.
A hash function takes data and produces a fixed-size fingerprint of it.
A hash can detect changes, but only when it is used inside a trustworthy integrity construction.
The qualification matters: hashing alone does not authenticate the sender.
If an attacker can change the data and also recompute the hash, the hash tells you nothing about who produced the message.
That brings us to two tools that do tie integrity to an identity or a key.
The first is the MAC, the message authentication code, and its common form, HMAC, the hash-based message authentication code.
A MAC or HMAC uses a shared key.
Anyone holding that key can produce or verify the code, so it proves the message came from someone holding the key and was not altered.
The second tool is the digital signature.
A digital signature verifies origin and integrity using asymmetric keys.
Hold on to the contrast: MAC and HMAC rely on a shared key, while a digital signature relies on a public and private key pair.
One question remains: how do you know that a public key really belongs to the party you think it does?
This is the job of PKI, public key infrastructure.
PKI binds public keys to identities through certificates, and those certificates are issued by trusted certification authorities, the CAs.
In short, a certificate says that this public key belongs to this identity, and a CA you trust vouches for that claim.
Now we apply these ideas to TLS, Transport Layer Security.
TLS protects communication above the transport layer.
It provides confidentiality, meaning the data is hidden from eavesdroppers, and integrity, meaning tampering is detected.
It also normally provides server authentication, so the client can be confident about which server it is talking to.
Mutual TLS goes further and adds client authentication, so that the server also verifies the client.
Let us walk through a modern handshake in order.
First, the endpoints negotiate parameters.
Second, they authenticate, using certificate signatures.
Third, they establish shared session keys.
Fourth, they exchange encrypted application data.
Notice how the earlier ideas fit together: asymmetric methods and certificates establish trust and keys, and then the shared session keys protect the actual data.
When a client receives a certificate, it must validate several things.
It validates the chain to a trusted CA.
It checks the hostname, so the certificate matches the server you intended to reach.
It checks the validity, meaning the certificate is within its valid period.
And it checks applicable revocation and policy.
There is a firm rule here: never disable verification to fix a certificate error.
A certificate error is the system warning you that authentication has failed, and switching verification off removes the very protection TLS is there to give.
A note on terminology.
SSL is obsolete terminology for older, insecure protocols.
Today the correct name is TLS.
And HTTPS is simply HTTP over TLS.
Finally, a classic misconception, which the source records as the historical pre-test misconception.
The belief is that strong AES alone prevents a man-in-the-middle attack, a MitM.
It does not.
If the endpoints are not authenticated, an attacker can establish separate encrypted sessions, one with each side.
Each session is strongly encrypted, yet the attacker sits in the middle and can read or alter everything.
Encryption strength is not the same as knowing who is at the other end.
That is why authentication matters.
Now to IPsec, which secures IP traffic itself.
IPsec has two main protocols.
ESP, the Encapsulating Security Payload, commonly provides confidentiality and integrity or authentication.
AH, the Authentication Header, provides integrity and authentication but without confidentiality, and it has complications with NAT, network address translation.
IPsec also has two modes.
In transport mode, the protection applies to the upper-layer payload.
In tunnel mode, IPsec encapsulates an original IP packet inside a new one.
Tunnel mode is common for site-to-site VPNs.
For setup, IKEv2, Internet Key Exchange version 2, authenticates the peers and negotiates security associations and keys.
A security association is the agreed set of parameters that governs the protection.
NAT traversal supports appropriate deployments where NAT sits in the path.
Now the VPN, the virtual private network.
A VPN connects sites or remote users across untrusted networks.
Two limits are worth remembering.
Tunnel encryption does not authorise every application, so access control is still needed on top.
And it does not protect compromised endpoints: if a device at either end is compromised, the tunnel will faithfully carry whatever that device sends.
Last, SSH, Secure Shell.
SSH provides authenticated, encrypted remote administration.
Good practice has four parts.
Validate the host key, so you know you are connecting to the intended machine.
Prefer managed key authentication.
Restrict administrative access.
And log actions, so there is a record of what was done.
Finally, do not confuse SSH with TLS or IPsec.

They all use cryptography, but they are different protocols with different roles: SSH is for remote administration, TLS protects communication above transport such as HTTPS, and IPsec secures IP traffic itself.
